chief_complaint: depressed mood, fatigue, worthlessness, PHQ-9 score 18
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with depressed mood, fatigue, worthlessness, phq-9 score 18. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she is suffering from severe physical exhaustion and a vitamin deficiency brought on by university burnout.
concerns: She is worried that falling behind on her coursework will cause her to fail the semester and waste the college tuition her parents saved for her.
expectations: She hopes to have blood work done to check for vitamin deficiencies and receive a medical excuse note for assignment extensions at university.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Major Depressive Disorder evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Major Depressive Disorder is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Confirm that symptoms meet duration, symptom-count, impairment, and exclusion criteria before diagnosing MDD; a PHQ-9 supports screening and severity assessment but is not diagnostic by itself.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: depressed mood, fatigue, worthlessness, PHQ-9 score 18

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with depressed mood, fatigue, worthlessness, phq-9 score 18. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Obtain vital signs, focused physical and mental-status examination, and an urgent suicide-risk assessment including intent, plan, means, past attempts, protective factors, psychosis, agitation, intoxication, and ability to maintain safety.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Major Depressive Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bipolar depression without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Failing to determine intent, plan, access to lethal means, prior attempts, protective factors, or whether emergency evaluation, observation, or hospitalization is needed.
Starting an antidepressant without screening for past mania/hypomania, psychosis, substance use, pregnancy potential, drug interactions, or medical contributors such as thyroid disease.
Not arranging early follow-up and counseling about activation, worsening agitation, or emergent suicidal thoughts after initiating an antidepressant in a young adult.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Active suicidal ideation with plan.
management_principles: If imminent suicide risk, psychosis, inability to maintain safety, or severe functional deterioration is identified, arrange emergency psychiatric evaluation and do not leave the patient alone; collaborate on a safety plan and lethal-means restriction when outpatient care is appropriate.

Screen for bipolar-spectrum illness before antidepressant monotherapy. If MDD is confirmed and outpatient treatment is appropriate, offer evidence-based psychotherapy and shared decision-making about an SSRI; counsel on expected onset, common adverse effects, activation, and urgent return precautions.

Arrange close follow-up, particularly after treatment initiation or dose changes, and obtain targeted tests (for example TSH, CBC/CMP, pregnancy test) only when history or examination suggests a medical contributor or medication safety need.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 20-year-old woman with recently worsening depressed mood, fatigue, worthlessness, and PHQ-9 score 18. Establish whether symptoms have persisted for at least two weeks, cause impairment, and meet full MDD criteria; assess anhedonia, neurovegetative symptoms, concentration, psychosis, prior episodes, mania/hypomania, substances, and medical contributors.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vital signs, focused physical and mental-status examination, and suicide-risk assessment including ideation, intent, plan, means, attempts, protective factors, psychosis, intoxication, and ability to maintain safety. Order targeted testing when clinically indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: Depressive episode; MDD is a leading diagnosis but cannot be confirmed until duration, symptom count, impairment, bipolar-spectrum history, substance/medication causes, and medical causes are assessed.
reference_soap.plan: If imminent safety risk, psychosis, or inability to maintain safety is present, arrange emergency psychiatric evaluation and consider hospitalization. Otherwise make a collaborative safety plan with lethal-means counseling, offer psychotherapy, and—after bipolar screening and shared decision-making—consider an SSRI with counseling about activation and emergent suicidal thoughts. Arrange early follow-up and escalation for worsening symptoms.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Major Depressive Disorder
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Major Depressive Disorder
Implement evidence-based management plan: Initiate Escitalopram 10mg daily, refer for CBT

teaching.one_liner: Persistent depressed mood and pervasive anhedonia lasting at least two weeks, severely impairing daily psychosocial functioning.

must_ask.say: Have you been feeling down or lost interest in things you used to enjoy, most days?
How has your sleep, appetite, and energy been?
Do you feel worthless, or excessively guilty about things?
Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn't worth living?
How long has this been going on, and how is it affecting school or work?

must_ask.objective: Suicide risk, means, and protective factors
must_ask.say: When you have thoughts of death or self-harm, have you thought about a plan or have access to anything you could use? What has helped keep you safe?

must_ask.objective: Bipolar and substance screen before antidepressants
must_ask.say: Have you ever had periods of needing very little sleep with unusually high energy, racing thoughts, risky behavior, or elevated mood? Have alcohol, drugs, or new medicines affected your mood?

history.answer: I've been feeling really down and exhausted lately, and I just can't seem to shake this heavy feeling.
It started about a month ago, and over the last three weeks it has been there almost every single day from morning until night.
There was no specific crisis or bereavement, but college coursework has been piling up and I felt completely overwhelmed.
Yes, almost all day every day I feel this deep sadness and empty feeling inside.
I completely lost interest in drawing and hanging out with my friends, which used to be my favorite hobbies.
I struggle to fall asleep until two or three in the morning, and then I wake up around five without feeling rested.
I have barely had any appetite for the past few weeks, and I noticed I lost about three kilograms.
I feel physically drained all day, and I have trouble focusing during lectures or making even small decisions.
I keep feeling like a complete failure and a burden to my parents and friends, even though I know they care about me.
My roommate told me that I seem to talk and move in slow motion compared to how I usually am.
Sometimes when it feels too heavy, I find myself wishing I wouldn't wake up in the morning, but I have not harmed myself.
No, I don't have any plan, method, or intent to kill myself, and I have never tried to commit suicide.
No, I don't keep any weapons, stockpiled pills, or dangerous items in my room.
My parents and my friends mean everything to me, and I came here today because I want to get better.
I've skipped several classes and fallen behind on homework because just getting out of bed feels exhausting.
No, I have never had times when I felt unusually high, needed very little sleep, or went on reckless spending sprees.
No, I haven't heard any voices or sounds that aren't there, and I don't feel like anyone is watching or plotting against me.
I only drink one glass of beer once or twice a month socially, and I don't use sleeping pills or illegal drugs.
No, I haven't noticed cold sensitivity, unusual constipation, neck swelling, or hair thinning.
No, I have never been pregnant and have never given birth.
I felt stressed during high school exam periods, but I've never experienced anything this prolonged or severe, and I've never received psychiatric treatment.
I thought maybe I'm just completely burnt out from university and dealing with some kind of severe vitamin deficiency.
I'm really worried that I'll end up flunking out of school this semester and waste all the tuition money my parents worked so hard to save.
I was hoping to have my blood checked for vitamin deficiencies and get a doctor's note for my professors so I can get an extension on my coursework.
I don't have any chronic medical illnesses like asthma, high blood pressure, or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, herbs, or nutritional supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I am a second-year university student, and I live in the university dormitory with one roommate.
My maternal aunt was treated for depression several years ago, but there is no family history of bipolar disorder or suicide.
My last period was about two weeks ago, and my menstrual cycle has always been regular every twenty-eight days.
I am not sexually active right now, so there is no possibility that I could be pregnant.

Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; speech is slowed with soft tone and delayed latency; affect is constricted and depressed; thought process is linear without delusions or hallucinations; insight and judgment are preserved.
Normal-sized thyroid without enlargement, tenderness, nodules, or bruits.
Pink conjunctivae without pallor; non-icteric sclerae.
Normal skin texture and turgor with no rashes, dryness, or signs of self-harm marks on the arms or wrists.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds and no murmurs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles or wheezing.
No resting or action tremors, tics, or abnormal involuntary movements observed.
